# Narrative Summary

I turned Seattle's transit system into a network and asked a simple question with
real stakes: **if the busiest stops or the key transfer points fail, how much does
the network fragment — and where are its hidden chokepoints?** Each stop in the
King County Metro schedule feed is a node, and a tie joins two stops that a vehicle
serves back-to-back on the same trip. Working with this network of 6,271 stops and
7,025 ties, I measured its basic structure (degree, clustering, components, path
lengths), ranked stops by betweenness centrality to find the bridges that hold
distant neighborhoods together, and then stress-tested the network by deleting
stops three different ways — at random, in decreasing degree order, and in
decreasing betweenness order — while tracking how the largest connected piece
shrinks.

Two findings stand out. First, the network's biggest chokepoint is not downtown
Seattle, where parallel routes give riders many options, but the **SR 520
floating-bridge corridor** across Lake Washington: all five of the
highest-betweenness stops in the region sit on that one corridor, and most of them
have only a handful of connections. Second, the fragmentation test **contradicts
the textbook expectation** for hub-dominated networks. Removing the
highest-*degree* stops broke the network fastest — after deleting just 5% of
stops, the largest connected piece fell from 99.5% to about 42% of stops — ahead
of betweenness-targeted removal (which halved the network at about 14% removed)
and random removal (about 17%). Seattle's transit network turns out to be a system
of long chains held together by a thin layer of modest junctions, and that
structure, more than any single hub, explains how it fails.

# Setup: Packages, Data, and Building the Graph

## Packages

```{r packages}
library(readr)     # reading the CSV files
library(dplyr)     # data wrangling
library(tidyr)     # reshaping data for plots
library(tibble)    # tidy tables
library(igraph)    # network analysis
library(ggraph)    # network visualization (ggplot2-based)
library(ggplot2)   # general plotting
```

## About the data

The data come from the **King County Metro General Transit Feed Specification
(GTFS) schedule feed**, published by King County Metro Transit and available at
<https://metro.kingcounty.gov/GTFS/google_transit.zip> (mirror:
<https://www.soundtransit.org/GTFS-KCM/google_transit.zip>). I downloaded the feed
on **November 18, 2026**; it is version **FAL26-161.5**, covering scheduled service
from **October 29, 2026 to March 26, 2027**. GTFS is the standard open format
transit agencies use to publish schedules; this feed covers Metro Transit bus,
Seattle Streetcar, King County Water Taxi, Sound Transit Link light rail, and
some Sound Transit Express service (142 routes and 31,484 trips in total). Because
GTFS is *published schedule* data, the network represents scheduled service
structure — not observed ridership or real-time operations.

From the feed I built two tidy tables (the conversion script sorts
`stop_times.txt` by trip and stop sequence and links each stop to the next one):

- **`nodes.csv`** — one row per stop: `id`, `name`, `x`/`y` (longitude/latitude),
  plus precomputed `degree` and `betweenness` used for checking.
- **`edges.csv`** — one row per tie: `from`, `to` (stop ids served consecutively
  on at least one trip).

The network is **one-mode, undirected, and unweighted**: a tie means "a vehicle
travels directly between these two stops," in either direction. In the graph,
**vertices are stops and edges are consecutive-stop links**.

> Data credit (required by King County): *Transit scheduling, geographic, and
> real-time data provided by permission of King County.*

## Building the graph

```{r build-graph}
nodes <- read_csv("nodes.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
edges <- read_csv("edges.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

g <- graph_from_data_frame(d = edges, vertices = nodes, directed = FALSE)

g
```

The graph has **6,271 nodes** and **7,025 ties**. One data-cleaning caveat, which
I return to in the sensitivity check below: these counts use raw stop IDs, and
the same physical stop is often split into several stop IDs by direction or bay.

# First Look: Visualizing the Network

## The geographic network, sized by betweenness

The plot below uses each stop's real longitude and latitude, so the network keeps
the shape of the city. Node **size shows betweenness centrality** (how often a
stop lies on shortest routes between other stops) and node **color shows degree**
(how many direct connections a stop has). The five highest-betweenness stops are
ringed in red.

```{r geo-plot, fig.width=9, fig.height=9}
V(g)$betweenness_r <- betweenness(g, directed = FALSE, normalized = TRUE)
top5 <- V(g)$name[order(-V(g)$betweenness_r, V(g)$name)][1:5]
V(g)$is_top5 <- V(g)$name %in% top5

ggraph(g, layout = "manual", x = V(g)$x, y = V(g)$y) +
  geom_edge_link(alpha = 0.25, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_node_point(aes(size = betweenness_r, colour = degree)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(filter = is_top5), shape = 21, size = 9,
                  stroke = 1.4, colour = "red", fill = NA) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(option = "plasma", name = "Degree") +
  scale_size_continuous(name = "Betweenness", range = c(0.4, 7)) +
  labs(title = "Seattle transit: the SR 520 bridge corridor is the chokepoint",
       subtitle = "Node size = betweenness; colour = degree; red rings = top 5 betweenness stops",
       caption = "King County Metro GTFS FAL26-161.5. Data provided by permission of King County.") +
  theme_graph()
```

The geography tells the story at a glance. The network is dense on the west side
(Seattle itself) and thins into long suburban chains to the east and south. The
red-ringed stops all sit on the **SR 520 corridor** at the east end of the
floating bridge — the main crossing of Lake Washington. Notice, too, that the
biggest dots are *not* the yellowest ones: the bridge stops have modest degree
(mostly 4–7) but enormous betweenness. They are brokers, not hubs.

## The degree distribution: beads on a string

```{r degree-dist, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.5}
tibble(degree = degree(g)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = degree)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "#4C72B0", colour = "white") +
  labs(title = "Degree distribution of Seattle transit stops",
       x = "Degree (number of direct connections)", y = "Number of stops") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The distribution is the opposite of a hub-dominated "scale-free" network:
**84% of stops have degree exactly 2** — they are simply the stop before and the
stop after on a route, like beads on a string. The average degree is 2.24 and the
maximum is only 14 (South Kirkland Park & Ride). Only 382 stops have degree 4 or
more. This chain-like structure is the key to everything that follows.

# Analysis

## Basic structure

```{r basic-stats}
n_components   <- components(g)$no
largest_share  <- max(components(g)$csize) / vcount(g)
clustering_avg <- transitivity(g, type = "average")
diam_lcc       <- diameter(g, directed = FALSE)          # on the largest component in practice
avg_path       <- mean_distance(g, directed = FALSE)

tibble(
  Measure = c("Nodes", "Ties", "Components", "Largest component share",
              "Average clustering", "Diameter (stops)", "Average shortest path (stops)"),
  Value   = c(vcount(g), ecount(g), n_components,
              round(largest_share, 4), round(clustering_avg, 4),
              diam_lcc, round(avg_path, 2))
)
```

The network is essentially one connected system — the largest component holds
**99.47%** of stops — with three tiny exceptions discussed below. Clustering is
very low (0.014): stops along a route almost never close into triangles, because
transit lines are chains, not cliques. Trips are long in stop terms: the average
shortest path is about **29 stops**, and the diameter is **93 stops**, reflecting
how far the suburban chains extend.

The four components are themselves informative. Besides the mainland network
(6,238 stops), there is a separate Vashon Island bus component (29 stops, linked
to the mainland only by ferry in the real world) and two 2-stop Water Taxi
components. The Water Taxi split is a *modeling artifact*: the two routes share
Colman Dock in reality, but the feed gives the dock different stop IDs per route,
so the graph cannot see the walking transfer. I keep this limitation visible
rather than hiding it, because it shows how data conventions become network
structure.

## Betweenness: finding the bridges

```{r betweenness-table}
tibble(stop = V(g)$name,
       betweenness = round(V(g)$betweenness_r, 3),
       degree = degree(g)) %>%
  arrange(desc(betweenness)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10)
```

The top of the ranking is dominated by one corridor: **SR 520 & 92nd Ave NE**
(betweenness ≈ 0.195, degree 6) and the Evergreen Point stops at the bridge's
east end. Six of the top 20 stops are on SR 520; a second cluster sits in the
Renton corridor. **No downtown Seattle or Link light rail station appears in the
top 20.** Downtown looks important, but its many parallel routes spread shortest
paths across dozens of stops, so no single downtown stop is critical. The
fragility lives in the suburbs, where one bridge or one arterial carries
everything.

The ranking also confirms the "broker" pattern: stops like **Bellevue Transit
Center – Bay 6** have degree only **2** yet rank in the top 10 by betweenness.
A degree-only analysis would call that stop unimportant; betweenness reveals it
as a load-bearing joint between chains.

## The resilience test: three ways to break the network

Now the central experiment. I delete stops in 1% steps up to 50% removed, under
three strategies:

- **Random** failure (mean of 10 trials) — models everyday disruptions;
- **Degree-targeted** — remove the best-connected stops first;
- **Betweenness-targeted** — remove the biggest bridges first.

After each step I record the size of the largest remaining component, as a
fraction of the original 6,271 stops.

```{r resilience}
set.seed(20261118)

largest_fraction <- function(graph) {
  if (vcount(graph) == 0) return(0)
  max(components(graph)$csize) / vcount(g)
}

attack_curve <- function(order_names, steps = 0:50) {
  sapply(steps, function(p) {
    k <- floor(p / 100 * vcount(g))
    if (k == 0) return(largest_fraction(g))
    largest_fraction(delete_vertices(g, order_names[seq_len(k)]))
  })
}

steps <- 0:50
deg_order <- V(g)$name[order(-degree(g), V(g)$name)]
bet_order <- V(g)$name[order(-V(g)$betweenness_r, V(g)$name)]

resilience <- tibble(
  pct_removed = steps,
  `Degree-targeted`      = attack_curve(deg_order, steps),
  `Betweenness-targeted` = attack_curve(bet_order, steps),
  Random = rowMeans(replicate(10, attack_curve(sample(V(g)$name), steps)))
)

resilience %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-pct_removed, names_to = "Strategy", values_to = "Largest component") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = pct_removed, y = `Largest component`, colour = Strategy)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  labs(title = "Resilience: largest component vs. stops removed",
       x = "Stops removed (%)", y = "Largest component (fraction of original stops)",
       caption = "King County Metro GTFS FAL26-161.5. Data provided by permission of King County.") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**The result contradicts the standard textbook story.** In hub-dominated
(scale-free) networks, degree-targeted attack is devastating but *betweenness*
attacks are usually comparable, and random failure is nearly harmless. Here:

- **Degree-targeted removal fragments the network fastest**: the largest
  component drops below 50% at only **5% removed**, with about **42%** of stops
  still in the largest component at that point.
- **Betweenness-targeted** removal halves the network at about **14%** removed.
- **Random** removal halves it at about **17%** — the network is only modestly
  robust even to random failure, because with average degree 2.24 there is
  little redundancy anywhere.

One reproducibility note: thousands of stops share the same degree, so the exact
degree-attack curve depends on how ties within an order are broken. The orders
above break ties by stop name, which makes this page fully reproducible; the
*ranking* of the three strategies (degree fastest, then betweenness, then
random) is stable across tie-breaking choices, while the exact percentages move
by a few points.

Why does the degree attack win here? Because in this chain-like network the
high-degree stops are not a few superstar hubs — they are the *entire junction
layer* (all 382 stops with degree ≥ 4) that stitches the beads-on-a-string
routes into one system. Deleting them unzips the chains everywhere at once. The
top-betweenness stops, by contrast, sit *in series* along a few corridors like
SR 520: once the first bridge stop is removed, its neighbors' betweenness
collapses too, so a static betweenness attack spends many of its cuts re-cutting
corridors that are already severed. The structure of the network — chains plus a
thin junction layer — determines which attack hurts most.

## A second fragmentation measure: do trips survive, and at what cost?

Largest-component size says when the network *splits*; it does not say when it
stops being *usable*. As a second measure, I sampled 300 pairs of stops and, at
each removal step, recorded (a) the share of pairs still connected and (b) the
average shortest path among the pairs that survive.

```{r path-measure}
set.seed(20261118)
lcc <- induced_subgraph(g, names(which(components(g)$membership ==
                                       which.max(components(g)$csize))))
pair_sample <- replicate(300, sample(V(lcc)$name, 2), simplify = FALSE)

pair_stats <- function(order_names, steps = 0:50) {
  t(sapply(steps, function(p) {
    k <- floor(p / 100 * vcount(g))
    h <- if (k == 0) g else delete_vertices(g, order_names[seq_len(k)])
    d <- sapply(pair_sample, function(pr) {
      if (!all(pr %in% V(h)$name)) return(NA_real_)
      dd <- distances(h, v = pr[1], to = pr[2])[1, 1]
      ifelse(is.infinite(dd), NA_real_, dd)
    })
    c(share_connected = mean(!is.na(d)), avg_path = mean(d, na.rm = TRUE))
  }))
}

path_deg <- pair_stats(deg_order)
path_bet <- pair_stats(bet_order)
# (Random strategy: average pair_stats() over several sampled orders.)

# Key rows, printed so the numbers quoted below can be checked against the code:
tibble(pct_removed = steps,
       degree_share_connected = round(path_deg[, "share_connected"], 3),
       degree_avg_path = round(path_deg[, "avg_path"], 1),
       betweenness_share_connected = round(path_bet[, "share_connected"], 3),
       betweenness_avg_path = round(path_bet[, "avg_path"], 1)) %>%
  filter(pct_removed %in% c(0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 15, 20))
```

Two lessons come from this measure. First, **pair connectivity collapses even
faster than the largest component**: the share of sampled pairs still connected
falls below 50% at roughly 4% removed (degree), 7% (betweenness), and 8%
(random), because a trip fails if *either* endpoint is removed *or* the path is
cut. Second, **trips get much longer before they become impossible**: under the
betweenness attack, the average path among surviving pairs stretches from about
30 stops to a peak of roughly **94 stops** at ~6% removed — cutting bridges
forces enormous detours along the chains — while random removal barely stretches
paths at all (peak ≈ 34). One honest caveat: after the peak, average path length
*falls* again, which is not recovery — it is survivorship. Eventually only short
local trips remain possible at all. The two panels of this analysis must always
be read together: **largest component says when the network splits; path length
says when it stops being usable — and usability fails first.**

## Sensitivity check: does merging duplicate stops change the answer?

The counts above use raw stop IDs, but agencies split one physical stop into
several IDs by direction or bay — visibly, *Sr 520 & Evergreen Point Rd* holds
both the #2 and #3 betweenness ranks. The feed's `parent_station` field, the
usual merging key, is blank for all 6,271 stops in this feed, so I merged stops
by **identical name plus coordinates rounded to 3 decimal places** instead:

```{r merge-check}
nodes_merged <- nodes %>%
  mutate(key = paste(name, round(x, 3), round(y, 3))) %>%
  group_by(key) %>%
  summarise(id_new = first(id), x = mean(x), y = mean(y), .groups = "drop")

id_map <- nodes %>%
  mutate(key = paste(name, round(x, 3), round(y, 3))) %>%
  left_join(nodes_merged %>% select(key, id_new), by = "key") %>%
  select(id, id_new)

edges_merged <- edges %>%
  left_join(id_map, by = c("from" = "id")) %>% rename(from_new = id_new) %>%
  left_join(id_map, by = c("to" = "id"))   %>% rename(to_new = id_new) %>%
  filter(from_new != to_new) %>%
  distinct(from = from_new, to = to_new)

g_merged <- graph_from_data_frame(edges_merged,
                                  vertices = nodes_merged %>% rename(id = id_new) %>%
                                    select(id, x, y),
                                  directed = FALSE)
c(nodes_merged = vcount(g_merged), ties_merged = ecount(g_merged),
  largest_share_merged = round(max(components(g_merged)$csize) / vcount(g_merged), 4))
```

Merging absorbs 881 duplicate stop IDs, giving **5,390 nodes and 6,976 ties** —
but the largest component still holds **99.46%** of stops, and the corridor
chokepoints are unchanged. The headline results are therefore not an artifact of
the stop-ID convention; I report the raw-ID network as the primary analysis
because it is the feed's own unit, with the merged network as the robustness
check.

# What Readers Should Take Away

Seattle's transit network is not held together by its biggest hubs; it is held
together by a **thin layer of modest junctions and a few load-bearing bridges**,
strung between long chains of ordinary stops. That structure produces a specific
kind of fragility. Everyday random failures are survivable but not cheap, because
a chain network has little redundancy anywhere. The catastrophic failures are
concentrated and predictable: lose the junctions and the system unzips into
hundreds of stranded fragments (removing just 5% of stops by degree cuts the
largest connected piece from 99.5% to about 42% of the network); lose the SR 520 bridge stops and cross-lake trips do not just fail —
the surviving ones balloon from ~30 stops to ~90. For a transit agency, the
practical lesson is that resilience planning should protect *brokers and
junctions*, not just busy stations: the stop that matters most may have only two
connections and a name nobody recognizes, right up until the day it closes.

Methodologically, this project is also a caution against importing textbook
expectations into real networks. The famous "robust to random failure, fragile
to targeted attack" result assumes a hub-dominated degree distribution that this
network simply does not have — and assuming it would have misidentified both the
most dangerous attack and the reason it works. The network's own structure,
measured first, has to dictate the hypotheses.

---

*Data: King County Metro GTFS feed, version FAL26-161.5, downloaded November 18,
2026, from <https://metro.kingcounty.gov/GTFS/google_transit.zip>. Transit
scheduling, geographic, and real-time data provided by permission of King County.
Analysis and visualization in R with igraph and ggraph; exploratory verification
of the feed counts was done in Python (networkx/pandas).*
